blocks.prompt: 3 (i) Prove from the first principle that: \({}^{n}P_{r} = n \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
blocks.explanation:
This is a proof, not a calculation.
We must show both sides are equal for all \(1 \le r \le n\).
Plan: start from the basic formula \({}^{n}P_{r} = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\), simplify the right side until it becomes the left side, then give the counting reason.
steps:
Given: \(n\) different objects, \(1 \le r \le n\).
To prove: \({}^{n}P_{r} = n \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
Method: First principle = the basic formula \({}^{n}P_{r} = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\). Start with the right side because it has more parts to simplify.

Multiply by \(n\)
\[\text{R.H.S.} = n \cdot \dfrac{(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}\]
\[= \dfrac{n(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}\]
\[= \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!}\]
Why: \(n \cdot (n-1)! = n!\), by the definition of factorial (e.g. \(5 \cdot 4! = 5!\)).

Reach the left side
\[\dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!} = {}^{n}P_{r} = \text{L.H.S.}\]
Why: This is exactly the formula for \({}^{n}P_{r}\).

Counting reason (why it is true)
To arrange \(r\) of the \(n\) objects, fill the first place in \(n\) ways. Then \(r - 1\) places remain and \(n - 1\) objects are left, which can be arranged in \({}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\) ways. By the fundamental principle of counting the total is \(n \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
Why: Both methods count the same arrangements, so they agree.

Check with numbers
\(n = 5\), \(r = 3\):
\[{}^{5}P_{3} = 60\]
\[5 \cdot {}^{4}P_{2} = 5 \times 12 = 60 \;\checkmark\]
Why: A numerical test confirms the identity.

blocks.prompt: 3 (ii) Prove from the first principle that: \({}^{n}P_{r} = {}^{n-1}P_{r} + r \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
blocks.explanation:
Another proof: the right side is a sum of two permutations.
We must show it equals \({}^{n}P_{r}\) (for \(1 \le r \le n - 1\), so that \({}^{n-1}P_{r}\) has meaning).
Plan: write both terms by the formula, take the common factor \(\frac{(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}\), and simplify; then give the counting reason.
steps:
Given: \(n\) different objects, \(1 \le r \le n - 1\).
To prove: \({}^{n}P_{r} = {}^{n-1}P_{r} + r \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
Method: Use \({}^{n}P_{r} = \frac{n!}{(n-r)!}\) for each term and add the two fractions using \((n-r)! = (n-r)(n-r-1)!\).

Write both terms by the formula
\[{}^{n-1}P_{r} = \dfrac{(n-1)!}{(n-1-r)!}\]
\[{}^{n-1}P_{r-1} = \dfrac{(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}\]
Why: In the first, \(n - 1\) replaces \(n\). In the second, \((n-1)-(r-1) = n - r\).

Make the denominators the same
\[\dfrac{(n-1)!}{(n-r-1)!} = \dfrac{(n-1)!\,(n-r)}{(n-r)!}\]
Why: \((n-r)! = (n-r)(n-r-1)!\), so multiply top and bottom by \((n - r)\).

Add the two terms
\[\text{R.H.S.} = \dfrac{(n-1)!\,(n-r)}{(n-r)!} + \dfrac{r\,(n-1)!}{(n-r)!}\]
\[= \dfrac{(n-1)!\,[(n-r) + r]}{(n-r)!}\]
Why: Same denominator, so add the tops; \((n-1)!\) is a common factor.

Simplify
\[= \dfrac{(n-1)! \cdot n}{(n-r)!}\]
\[= \dfrac{n!}{(n-r)!} = {}^{n}P_{r}\]
Why: \((n - r) + r = n\), and \(n \cdot (n-1)! = n!\).

Counting reason (why it is true)
Fix one particular object, say \(A\). Every arrangement of \(r\) objects either leaves \(A\) out or uses \(A\).
Without \(A\): arrange \(r\) of the other \(n - 1\) objects: \({}^{n-1}P_{r}\) ways.
With \(A\): \(A\) takes one of the \(r\) places (\(r\) ways), and the other \(r - 1\) places are filled from \(n - 1\) objects: \({}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\) ways, so \(r \cdot {}^{n-1}P_{r-1}\).
Why: The two cases do not overlap and together cover every arrangement, so we add them.

Check with numbers
\(n = 5\), \(r = 3\):
\[{}^{4}P_{3} + 3 \cdot {}^{4}P_{2} = 24 + 36\]
\[= 60 = {}^{5}P_{3} \;\checkmark\]
Why: Both sides give 60.
